rows.title: Color
rows.text: Cattle, goats, sheep and horses have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three, and you very likely have two as well. In the white-tailed deer, one kind senses blue light best, and in the fallow deer the other kind senses green light best.
rows.note: R6 (white-tailed deer) says cones and rods but gives no cone count, so I did not say deer were measured to have two kinds. Peak wavelengths left out as numbers.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: Your eyes sit on the sides of your head, so each one looks out in a different direction. Nobody has measured how wide an area you see at once, or how much of it both of your eyes see together in front of you. Both have been measured in cattle, goats, giraffes and horses, but in no deer.

cites.taxon: Cervidae (deer, as the page states it)

rows.note: Left out the 310 degree figure (R10): it is an unsourced book line about deer in general, and field widths may only carry within a genus.

rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: Your pupil, the opening that lets light into your eye, is a horizontal slit if you are a white-tailed deer, a red deer, a moose or a caribou. If you are a caribou, the slit opens into a round shape with about thirteen times the area when your pupil is fully open. Nobody has recorded the pupil of mule deer, roe deer or fallow deer.
rows.note: Pupil shape is unrecorded for mule, roe and fallow deer, so the row says so; the area figure is caribou only.

rows.title: Sharpness, dim light and depth
rows.text: If you are a white-tailed deer, you see four to six cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30, so fine detail is much blurrier for you. A reflective layer called the tapetum covers the upper part of your eye and overlaps the horizontal streak where you see most sharply. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see by, or how well you judge depth.
rows.note: Acuity and tapetum are measured only in white-tailed deer here; dim-light sensitivity and depth have no deer record, so the row says so.
